citations.narrative:
The facility is failing to maintain their veterinary hospital that houses the Black Vulture in good repair. At the time of the
inspection, the APHIS official observed approximately three inches of standing water in the hospital hallway and offices.
The building smelled strongly of mold. The ceiling of the hallway and office had wet insulation hanging down and exposed
rotten wood. The ceiling area in front of the sheltered housing for the Black Vulture enclosure was patched with plywood
and smelled of mold. The roof has a hole that is approximately two feet in diameter. The roofing tiles are missing in some
areas with the gutters pulling away from the roof. The treatment room smells of mold with black fuzzy organic material
visible in the corner near the scale.
The facility stated they haven’t been able to receive enough roofing bids to move forward with repairs. The roof has been
in disrepair for over three months. Housing facilities for birds must be designed and constructed so that they are
structurally sound for the species of bird housed in them. They must be kept in good repair and protect the birds from
injury.
Correct by: September 30, 2026

citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility does not have appropriate facilities to comply with the Animal Welfare Regulations. The veterinary hospital is
in disrepair. At the time of the inspection, there were three inches of standing water inside the building. The ceiling above
the hallway is deteriorated with exposed wet wood beams and insulation is hanging down. The APHIS official could smell
a strong mold odor. The hospital office ceiling is also deteriorated with exposed wet beams and insulation hanging down.
The hallway in front of the animal enclosures is missing ceiling tiles. The missing tiles have created a hole which is
approximately three feet by two feet exposing the wood beams and insulation.
The hospital treatment room, which also has standing water and a moldy odor, is used to store the facility’s medications.
The controlled drug lockbox on the floor is flooded and unable to be used. There are rodent feces and nesting materials
on top of the electrical box. The ceiling is discolored with fuzzy black organic material. The floor behind the metal exam
table is discolored with fuzzy black organic material. There are rodent feces in the corner of the room behind the
treatment equipment. The APHIS official could smell a strong mold odor throughout the hospital.
The roof of the building has a hole that is approximately two feet in diameter. The roofing tiles are missing in some areas
with the gutters pulling away from the roof. The facility stated they haven’t been able to receive enough roofing bids to
move forward with repairs.
The licensee must establish and maintain a program of adequate veterinary care that includes the availability of
appropriate facilities, personnel, equipment, and services to comply with the provisions of the Animal Welfare
Regulations.
Correct by: October 30, 2026

citations.desc: Attending veterinarian and adequate veterinary care (dealers and exhibitors).
citations.narrative:
The facility is maintaining expired Ciprofloxacin, Meloxicam, Sucralfate, Epinephrine, Dexamethasone, and Noromectin in
their pharmacy available for use for regulated animals. The use of expired medications is not consistent with standard
veterinary care and is in appropriate to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries since the expected
results cannot be guaranteed. The licensee must establish and maintain a program of adequate veterinary care that
includes the use of appropriate methods to prevent, control, diagnose, and treat diseases and injuries.
Correct by: September 5, 2026

The facility has substantial evidence of pests.
In the animal diet preparation area and bedding storage building, the floor behind the bedding has a heavy accumulation
of rodent feces. There are rodent feces and urine on bags of unopened feed. The building also has an accumulation of
cobwebs behind feed storage and on the ceiling. This building stores food and bedding for all animals.
While the facility has instituted the use of rodent traps, it isn’t an effective method of pest control. The presence of insects
and mammal pests may create a disease hazard to the animals. A safe and effective program for the control of insects,
ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests shall be established and maintained.
Correct by: September 30, 2026

The facility is not maintaining the surfaces of housing facilities including perches in the Chimpanzee, Schmidts Guenon,
and Spider Monkey enclosures. The Chimpanzee perches have excessively rusted, bent bars supporting the wood
planks. One perch is bent and bowing from the weight of the animal from 90 degrees to approximately 45 degrees. At
least three of the perches have broken wood planks and one of the planks is no longer connected to the rusted support
bar putting the animals at risk for injury. The paint has peeled from the concrete door frame of the shift gate in the
individually housed Schmidts Guenon enclosure. The concrete surface is crumbling and is unable to be properly cleaned
and sanitized.
The Spider Monkey feed perch is made of wire. The wire sides have disconnected from the wire base causing a three-
inch gap. The gap puts the two spider monkeys at risk of animal entrapment.
The facility is not maintaining the shift doors for both the Chimpanzees and the Spider Monkeys; the doors are not free of
excessive rust. The outer areas of the metal shift doors are reddish brown and have a pockmarked appearance. The
metal bars attached to the cement wall that allow the door to shift open and closed are also a deep reddish brown with
pockmarked areas. The non-human primates can come into contact with the rusted surfaces. Rusted primary enclosure
surfaces can lose structural integrity over time and cannot be properly cleaned and sanitized.
The licensee must ensure that any surfaces that come into contact with non-human primates are free of excessive rust
that prevents the required cleaning and sanitization, or that affects the structural strength of the surfaces.
Correct by: September 30, 2026

At the time of the inspection, the inspector identified a backed-up drainage pipe in the Ruffed-Coat Lemur building. The
facility manager stated the drainage system in this building is clogged and is not functioning.
Improper drainage systems and standing water where the animals are contained may result in noxious odors, spreading
of diseases, insect infestation, and/or other health hazards. Housing facilities for non-human primates must be
constructed and maintained minimizing vermin and pest infestation, insects, odors, and disease hazards.
Correct by: October 31, 2026

At the time of the inspection, the facility failed to maintain adequate lighting in the indoor housing facility for the Schmidt’s
Guenon. The light in front of the enclosure wasn’t functioning properly, and the APHIS official had to utilize their flashlight
to conduct the inspection because the enclosure was too dark to adequately assess the animal or the enclosure. As a
result of the broken light, the guenon does not have a diurnal light cycle that is uniformly diffused throughout the animal
facilities. Adequate lighting is essential to ensure thorough cleaning, proper facility maintenance, and effective daily
monitoring of the primates. Indoor housing facilities must provide adequate lighting to permit routine inspection, cleaning
of the facility, and observation of the nonhuman primates. Animal areas must be provided with a regular diurnal lighting
cycle of either natural or artificial light. Lighting must be uniformly diffused throughout animal facilities and provide
sufficient illumination to aid in maintaining good housekeeping practices, adequate cleaning, adequate inspection of
animals, and for the well-being of the animals.
Correct by: September 15, 2026

The facility failed to maintain adequate lighting in the sheltered portion of the housing facility for the single housed Diana
Guenon and two spider Monkeys. The light in front of the enclosure wasn’t functioning, and the APHIS official had to
utilize their flashlight to conduct the inspection. The guenon and spider monkeys are not provided with a diurnal light cycle
that is uniformly diffused throughout the animal facilities. Adequate lighting is essential to ensure thorough cleaning,
proper facility maintenance, and effective daily monitoring of the primates. The sheltered part of sheltered housing must
be lighted enough to permit routine inspection, cleaning of the facility, and observation of the nonhuman primates. Animal
areas must be provided with a regular diurnal lighting cycle of either natural or artificial light. Lighting must be uniformly
diffused throughout animal facilities and provide sufficient illumination to aid in maintaining good housekeeping practices,
adequate cleaning, adequate inspection of animals, and for the well-being of the animals.
Correct by: September 15, 2026

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
The facility failed to maintain adequate housekeeping for the premises and surrounding grounds. Almost all the
enclosures on the property are surrounded by tall weeds, grass, and overgrown bushes. Many of the weeds and grasses
have grown to more than 10 feet in height around the enclosure housing a Colobus monkey. There are trees growing over
the Chimpanzee moat towards the island. The enclosure fences of the Colobus monkey cannot be visualized due to the
heavy plant overgrowth.
Tall weeds and grass provide nesting grounds and harborage for pests and vermin which can be harmful to the health
and well-being of the animals housed at the facility. They also hinder the ability to inspect enclosures for disrepair.
Premises, including the surrounding grounds, must be kept clean in order to facilitate husbandry practices and to reduce
or eliminate breeding and living areas for rodents, pests, and vermin. Weeds, grass, and bushes must be controlled to
facilitate cleaning of the premises and pest control.
Correct by: September 30, 2026

citations.desc: Cleaning, sanitization, housekeeping, and pest control.
citations.narrative:
At the time of the inspection, an APHIS official observed four dead cockroaches hanging from the light fixture in front of
the Diana Guenon enclosure. There was also a live cockroach in front of this enclosure.
Pests such as cockroaches and insects can introduce pathogens, parasites, and environmental contaminants that pose
direct health risks to animals. Contaminated feed or water can also diminish animal welfare, reduce nutritional quality, and
create stressful or unsafe living conditions.
The facility must develop an effective program for control of insects, external parasites, and birds and mammals that are
pests must be established and maintained so as to promote the health and well-being of the animals and reduce
contamination by pests in animal areas.
Correct by: September 30, 2026

The housing facilities are in disrepair in several areas.
At the time of the inspection, the APHIS official smelled an electrical burning odor in the Pygmy Hippopotamus building.
Upon further investigation by facility personnel, the odor was caused by a broken air conditioner. The facility must
maintain the air conditioner in good repair to prevent an electrical fire and injury or death to the animals.
Other areas of the Pygmy Hippopotamus enclosure are in disrepair. The metal framed doors have wood planking that is
severely deteriorated. The wood is splintered and has a hole approximately one foot by three feet in the center of the
door. Failure to have doors in good repair may result in entrapment, escape, or injury to the hippos.
The fence in the Pygmy Hippopotamus enclosure is also in disrepair. A tree fell on the fence dividing the outdoor area,
and the fence is currently half standing. Broken fencing can cause harm to animals.
The outdoor enclosure for 11 prairie dogs has broken wires creating sharp points. Sharp points can cause injury to the
prairie dogs.
Insulation was falling out of the ceiling in the Asian Bear building. The insulation was landing in front of the enclosure near
the fan that blows into the enclosure. Ingestion of insulation can cause injury to the bear.
The facility failed to maintain housing facilities for the beaver. The ceiling area in front of the sheltered housing for a
Beaver enclosure is partially patched with plywood and smelled of mold. The roof has a hole that’s approximately two feet
in diameter. The roofing tiles are missing in some areas with the gutters pulling away from the roof.
The facility stated they haven’t been able to receive enough roofing bids to move forward with repairs. The roof has been
in disrepair for over three months.
The facility shall maintain the housing facilities in good repair to protect the animals from escape and injury to ensure the
welfare of the animals.
Correct by: September 30, 2026

At the time of the inspection, the APHIS official observed a box of romaine lettuce with black and white slimy mold present
on the leaves. The facility is feeding this lettuce to most of the animals. There was also an opened tube of raw meat
(“Nebraska Canine Diet”) that was dark to medium brown in color with black crusty meat on the edges of the bag,
indicating it was spoiled. The facility is feeding this meat to the otter. Feeding deteriorating food to the animals can
negatively impact their health and well-being by causing foodborne illnesses. The food shall be wholesome, palatable,
and free from contamination and of sufficient quantity and nutritive value to maintain all animals in good health.
Correct by: August 30, 2026

The facility is failing to properly sanitize the Pygmy Hippopotamus indoor housing facilities. There is a buildup of brown
organic material approximately three feet up the walls. The facility stated they are sanitizing the enclosure weekly, but the
surfaces are not being cleaned often enough to prevent the buildup and debris.
The accumulation of brown organic material on all of the surfaces the regulated animals come in contact with can be a
source of bacteria and possible health issues for the animals.
Cages, rooms, and hard-surfaced pens or runs shall be sanitized either by washing them with hot water (180 F. at source)
and soap or detergent, as in a mechanical washer, or by washing all soiled surfaces with a detergent solution followed by
a safe and effective disinfectant, or by cleaning all soiled surfaces with saturated live steam under pressure. Pens or runs
using gravel, sand, or dirt, shall be sanitized when necessary, as directed by the attending veterinarian.
Correct by: September 15, 2025

The facility has substantial evidence of pests.
In the animal diet preparation area and bedding storage building, the floor behind the bedding has a heavy accumulation
of rodent feces. There are rodent feces and urine on bags of unopened feed. The building also has an accumulation of
cobwebs behind feed storage and on the ceiling. This building stores food and bedding for all animals.
In the pygmy hippo building, the inspector observed one live cockroach above the enclosure next the pygmy hippos and
multiple dead cockroaches hanging from light fixtures.
While the facility has instituted the use of rodent traps, it isn’t an effective method of pest control. The presence of insects
and mammal pests may create a disease hazard to the animals. A safe and effective program for the control of insects,
ectoparasites, and avian and mammalian pests shall be established and maintained.
Correct by: September 30, 2026

During the inspection, the facility manager stated that he does not have sufficient help to facilitate adequate animal care,
husbandry, cleaning, and maintenance of the facility. This is evident in numerous areas of the facility, as noted by the
areas of disrepair and ineffective pest control throughout the facility documented in this report. There are currently nine
employees to carry out all aspects of animal care for 85 animals.
Without adequate employees, animals and facilities cannot be properly managed, leading to circumstances that
compromise the health and well-being of the animals. A sufficient number of adequately trained employees shall be
utilized to maintain the professionally acceptable level of husbandry practices as set forth in the regulations.
Correct by: September 30, 2026
